defect.evidence_quote: Whether a temporary visitor present in another's home for a commercial transaction has a reasonable expectation of privacy entitling him to challenge a search of that home. ## Rule No.
defect.problem: The case identity and citation are verified, and the commercial-visitor/no-privacy proposition is supported in substance, but the quoted phrase "merely present with the consent of the householder" is not verifiable from any disclosed text or lake pinpoint.
defect.proposed_fix: Remove quotation marks around that phrase or add a matching Carter text/pinpoint.

reasons: Lake identity verifies Minnesota v. Carter, 525 U.S. 83, U.S. Supreme Court, 1998.
Lake pin-90 supports only the temporary commercial visitor/no expectation proposition in summary form; it does not contain the quoted words.
residual_risks: The full opinion text, not disclosed here, could validate the exact quotation.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Paraphrase the Carter boundary unless the exact quotation is backed by a disclosed pinpoint.

defect.evidence_quote: A camper has a reasonable expectation of privacy in a closed tent, and that expectation does not turn on whether he had permission to be on the public land.
defect.locator_note: United States v. Sandoval table row
defect.problem: The identity, citation, court/year, and main holding are supported, but the disposition phrase "denial of suppression reversed" is not expressly verifiable from the disclosed record.
defect.proposed_fix: Delete the disposition phrase or add a pinpoint showing reversal of the suppression denial.

reasons: Lake identity verifies United States v. Sandoval, 200 F.3d 659, Ninth Circuit, 2000.
Pin-661 supports a closed tent on BLM land and the rule that privacy does not turn on permission to be there.
residual_risks: The appellate disposition may be correct, but it is not shown in the disclosed excerpt.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: State the supported holding without the disposition unless a disposition source is added.

defect.locator_note: United States v. Ruckman table row
defect.problem: Only citation identity is disclosed for Ruckman; the cave/trespasser/no-expectation/open-land holding cannot be verified because the lake record is an under-review frontier stub with no pinpoints or opinion text.
defect.proposed_fix: Do not state the Ruckman holding or split role until a full record, pinpoint, or text file is disclosed.

reasons: Lake identity verifies United States v. Ruckman, 806 F.2d 1471, 10th Cir., 1986.
The record status is under_review, treatment validity is unverified, and pinpoints is empty.
residual_risks: The holding may be accurate in the actual opinion, but it is not confirmable from the disclosed evidence.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Limit this row to citation existence or replace it with a verified record before using it as split authority.

defect.evidence_quote: The district court did not err in concluding a tent is more like a house than a car. We hold that Gooch had a reasonable expectation of privacy such that the warrantless search of his tent violated the Fourth Amendment.
defect.locator_note: United States v. Gooch table row
defect.problem: Gooch supports the tent-search privacy holding, but the row also asserts a separate closed-tent "non-public" arrest-warrant holding that is not supported by the disclosed Gooch pinpoints; the quoted phrase also changes the source punctuation from a period to a comma.
defect.proposed_fix: Keep the supported search/interior holding, correct the quote punctuation, and add a separate Gooch pinpoint for the non-public/arrest-warrant claim or remove that clause.

reasons: Lake identity verifies United States v. Gooch, 6 F.3d 673, Ninth Circuit, 1993.
Pin-677b supports reasonable expectation and warrantless search violation, but no disclosed Gooch quote says "non-public" or states the arrest-warrant rule.
residual_risks: A missing full-opinion passage could support the arrest-warrant point.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Separate the search holding from the arrest-entry rule and support each with its own pinpoint.

defect.evidence_quote: a twofold requirement, first that a person have exhibited an actual (subjective) expectation of privacy and, second, that the expectation be one that society is prepared to recognize as 'reasonable.'
defect.locator_note: Katz v. United States table row
defect.problem: The case identity and Katz two-part test are supported, but the verbatim quote "the Fourth Amendment protects people, not places" is not present in the disclosed Katz pinpoints or any text file.
defect.proposed_fix: Remove the quote or add a disclosed Katz pinpoint containing the exact language.

reasons: Lake identity verifies Katz v. United States, 389 U.S. 347, U.S. Supreme Court, 1967.
Pin-361 supports the subjective/objective reasonable-expectation test; pin-351 only says the inquiry is personal, not spatial.
residual_risks: The quote may exist in the actual opinion, but it is not disclosed here.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Use the disclosed two-part-test language, or supply a pinpoint for the people-not-places quote.

defect.evidence_quote: Whether an overnight guest has a reasonable expectation of privacy in his host's home sufficient to challenge a warrantless entry. ## Rule Yes.
defect.problem: Olson verifies overnight-guest standing in a host's home, but the row generalizes that rule to "the place he is staying" and to another person's tent without disclosed authority for that extension.
defect.proposed_fix: Phrase the tent point as an analogy, not a verified Olson holding, unless separate tent-guest authority is added.

reasons: Lake identity verifies Minnesota v. Olson, 495 U.S. 91, U.S. Supreme Court, 1990.
Pin-98 supports a host-home overnight guest, not a tent-specific guest rule.
residual_risks: A separate case could extend Olson to tents, but none is disclosed in this row.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Say Olson supplies the home-guest analogy; do not state the tent application as established by Olson alone.

defect.evidence_quote: In terms that apply equally to seizures of property and to seizures of persons, the Fourth Amendment has drawn a firm line at the entrance to the house. Absent exigent circumstances, that threshold may not reasonably be crossed without a warrant.
defect.locator_note: Payton v. New York table row
defect.problem: Payton's firm-line quote is verified, but the row's claim that Gooch applied Payton to a closed tent as a non-public place needing an arrest warrant is not supported by the disclosed Gooch pinpoints.
defect.proposed_fix: Keep the Payton firm-line rule and add a verified Gooch pinpoint for the tent application, or remove the Gooch application from this row.

reasons: Lake identity verifies Payton v. New York, 445 U.S. 573, U.S. Supreme Court, 1980.
Payton pin-590 is matched and star-verified, but no disclosed Gooch passage contains the non-public/arrest-warrant application.
residual_risks: The Gooch application may be accurate, but it requires evidence outside the disclosed pinpoints.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Separate Payton's rule from any tent-specific application unless the Gooch application is independently pinned.

defect.evidence_quote: distinguished 'open fields' from the 'curtilage,' the land immediately surrounding and associated with the home,
defect.locator_note: Oliver v. United States table row
defect.problem: Oliver supports the open-fields/curtilage distinction and Basher supports no curtilage outside the tent, but the stronger claim that Oliver is the "doctrinal basis" for Basher is not expressly verified from disclosed Basher text.
defect.proposed_fix: Change "the doctrinal basis for Basher" to "the general open-fields/curtilage framework relevant to Basher" unless Basher text confirming reliance is added.

reasons: Lake identity verifies Oliver v. United States, 466 U.S. 170, U.S. Supreme Court, 1984.
Oliver treatment scope says it reaffirms the open-fields doctrine and curtilage distinction; Basher pin-1169a supports no expectation outside the tent.
residual_risks: Basher may cite Oliver directly, but that link is not disclosed.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Avoid asserting a direct doctrinal-basis relationship unless the Basher opinion text is available.

defect.evidence_quote: Good law in-circuit; reaffirms tent privacy while holding the area outside a dispersed-campsite tent is not curtilage.
defect.locator_note: United States v. Basher table row
defect.problem: Basher's no-curtilage/outside-the-tent holding is supported, but the direct quote "comparable to a house, apartment, or hotel room" is not present in the disclosed Basher pinpoints or text.
defect.proposed_fix: Use the lake treatment paraphrase or add a Basher pinpoint containing the exact comparative quote.

reasons: Lake identity verifies United States v. Basher, 629 F.3d 1161, Ninth Circuit, 2011.
Pin-1169a supports no expectation in the campsite/outside-tent area; the quoted comparable-to-home phrase is not disclosed.
residual_risks: The exact quote could be in the full opinion, but the full opinion text is not in the working directory.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Paraphrase Basher as reaffirming tent privacy unless the exact quote is pinned.

defect.evidence_quote: The district court did not err in concluding a tent is more like a house than a car. We hold that Gooch had a reasonable expectation of privacy such that the warrantless search of his tent violated the Fourth Amendment.
defect.problem: The core Gooch/Katz tent-interior rule has support, but the black-letter statement includes corpus-wide negative and comparative claims not verifiable from disclosed evidence: no Supreme Court tents decision, doctrine built in courts of appeals, and most heavily in the Ninth Circuit.
defect.proposed_fix: Remove or qualify the no-SCOTUS and most-heavily-Ninth-Circuit claims, or add disclosed evidence supporting those corpus-wide assertions and at least two affirmative approvals for the black-letter rule.

reasons: Gooch pin-677b supports the home-not-car comparison and warrantless tent-search violation.
Katz pin-361 supports the two-part reasonable-expectation test.
The disclosed files do not prove the negative claim that the Supreme Court has never addressed tents directly or the comparative claim that the doctrine is most heavily Ninth Circuit.
residual_risks: A complete corpus search could validate the negative and comparative claims, but searching is outside the disclosed-evidence universe.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Keep the Gooch/Katz supported rule, and move no-SCOTUS/Ninth-Circuit-weight claims to a sourced lower-court-development note.
